RagShortTexts: Neighbours negotiate paths, meadows, water and shared obligations under differing rights.
Cooperation does not imply periodic equal land division; kin and authority still matter.

Variants.Content:
Fields, house plots and meadows intertwine with neighbours’ paths and water. Driving stock past crops, clearing ditches, repairing a crossing or meeting a collective demand requires agreement over labour and materials. People who remember boundaries, kin and local notables mediate disputes; help for labour-poor homes creates obligations affecting the next season.

Shared work does not make every holding equal. Inheritance, lordly or church claims, tenancy, debt and marriage alter who cultivates land. A transfer requires identifying the cultivator, rent claimant and boundary. Treating communal work as permission to redistribute every field undermines investment and inflames kin disputes.
Stewards need to know each household’s animals and labour rather than hide differences under one levy. Recognising cultivation and rent claims supports future sowing.
Troops seeking carts must ask who can promise them and whether essential plough animals are involved. One elder’s consent may not bind every kin group.
Neighbours remember carts and labour contributed to road work. Assistance creates returns at haymaking, animal loans, weddings and funerals.
